This book covers AS topics 1.1 and 1.5.1–1.5.2: types of business entity, the accounting equation, preparing a statement of profit or loss and a statement of financial position for a sole trader, adjustments (accruals, prepayments, irrecoverable debts, allowance for irrecoverable debts, inventory valuation) and incomplete records. These are core to Paper 2 and Paper 1. In mark guides, (1) is one mark and OF means "own figure" (follow-through credit for correct method using an earlier wrong figure). Every calculation was checked by computer. The mark guides are our own and are not official Cambridge mark schemes.

Unit 1 of 10: Types of Business Entity

Key ideas

  • Sole trader: owned by one person; unlimited liability; easy to set up; profits kept by the owner; limited capital.
  • Partnership: two or more owners; shared capital, skills and risk; usually unlimited liability; governed by a partnership agreement (or, in its absence, rules such as those in the Partnership Act 1890).
  • Limited company: separate legal entity; owned by shareholders with limited liability; managed by directors; must publish accounts; raises capital by issuing shares.
  • Not-for-profit organisations: clubs and societies (A Level).
  • Business entity concept: the business is treated as separate from its owner(s) for accounting purposes.

Worked examples

Example 1: a sole trader's business owes $50 000 but has only $20 000 of assets; with unlimited liability, the owner's personal assets can be used to pay the remaining $30 000.

Example 2: a shareholder who paid $5000 for shares can lose at most $5000 if the company fails — limited liability.

Example 3: drawings of goods by a sole trader are recorded separately because of the business entity concept.

10-mark exam-style question

(a) Explain the meaning of unlimited liability. [2]

(b) Give two advantages and two disadvantages of operating as a sole trader. [4]

(c) Explain two reasons why a sole trader might convert the business into a limited company. [4]

Answers and mark guide:

  • (a) The owner is personally responsible for all the debts of the business (1); personal assets may be used to pay business debts (1).
  • (b) Advantages: full control; keeps all profits; simple to set up; privacy of accounts (1 each, max 2). Disadvantages: unlimited liability; limited capital; long hours/no one to share decisions; business may end on death of owner (1 each, max 2).
  • (c) Limited liability protects personal assets (1), reducing personal risk as the business grows (1); easier to raise capital by issuing shares (1), allowing expansion (1).

Common mistakes

  1. Saying sole traders cannot employ staff.
  2. Confusing shareholders with directors.
  3. Thinking partnerships always have limited liability.
  4. Forgetting the business entity concept.
  5. Listing points without explanation in "explain" questions.

Quick recall

  1. Define limited liability.
  2. Who manages a limited company?
  3. What governs a partnership if there is no agreement?
  4. Define the business entity concept.
  5. One advantage of a partnership over a sole trader?

Answers: 1) Owners' losses are limited to the amount invested. 2) Directors. 3) The Partnership Act 1890 (in this syllabus). 4) The business is treated as separate from its owners. 5) More capital/shared skills.
